say: Good morning, inquirers! Today we are cake cutters and pizza sharers. There is one rule: every share must be FAIR.
By the end you will name fair shares with fractions, tell which share is bigger, and explain how you know.
Look at each snack. Ali and Mei want to share it. Is it fair? Thumbs up for fair, thumbs down for not fair.
Be ready to tell me why.
Before we fold: which will be bigger, one quarter of a strip or one eighth of the same strip? Show me 4 fingers for a quarter or 8 fingers for an eighth.
stuck: Stuck folding: match the two ends exactly, then press the fold flat.
Not sure what to write: “How many equal parts are there? That number goes at the bottom.”
Finished early: can you fold a strip into 3 equal parts? How do you check they are equal?

say: “Before I name a fraction I check the parts are equal. This bar has 5 parts, all the same size, so the parts are fifths: 5 goes at the bottom. 3 parts are shaded: 3 goes on top. Three fifths.”
“One half or one sixth: which is bigger? Same whole. One half is 1 of 2 parts, one sixth is 1 of 6 parts. More parts means smaller parts, so one half is bigger.”
“Two ninths and four ninths: ninths are the name of the parts, like apples. 2 ninths and 4 ninths are 6 ninths. The parts do not change size, so the bottom number stays 9.”

do: Ask: “Are all the parts the same size? How do you know?”
Ask: “What does the bottom number tell us? What does the top number tell us?”
Ask: “Did you draw both wholes the same length?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Count all the equal parts first. That number goes at the bottom.”
Hint 2: “Fold or draw a strip to check which part is bigger.”
Hint 3: “Colour the parts on a bar, then count them.”

Ask: “Did you draw both wholes the same length?”

Hint 2: “Fold or draw a strip to check which part is bigger.”

say: “Is 1/2 always bigger than 1/4? Can you think of a time when it is not?”
ask: “Is 1/2 always bigger than 1/4? Can you think of a time when it is not?”
Only when the wholes are the same size: half a small cupcake is less than a quarter of a big cake.

say: “You checked for equal parts, compared fractions with bars and explained why. That is fair and careful maths.”

p2l7-title.note: Objective: Recognise equal parts and name fractions (halves, thirds, quarters, up to twelfths); compare unit fractions and like fractions; add and take away like fractions within one whole; solve fair-sharing stories with a bar. Materials: 4 paper strips of the same length per child (A4 cut lengthwise), paper circles, scissors, crayons, mini whiteboards. Online: each child has 4 paper strips, a crayon and scissors on camera; the tutor shows fraction bars on the slides. Time plan: opening 0 to 1.5, sneak-peek puzzles 1.5 to 6, warm-up 6 to 10.5, explore 10.5 to 23.5, mini-lesson 23.5 to 35.5, brain break 35.5 to 38.5, worksheet page 1 38.5 to 52.5, check together, page 1 52.5 to 55, short teaching 55 to 59.5, worksheet page 2 59.5 to 71, check together, page 2 71 to 73.5, flex (spare time) 73.5 to 76.5, talk time 76.5 to 81.5, exit ticket 81.5 to 86.5, looking back 86.5 to 88.5, closing and stamps 88.5 to 90. The Think harder and Go further slides are optional, if you finish early (no clock time). Kit ready at minute 0: ask families to put every item on the desk before the lesson starts (a 30-second check at the start).

p2l7-precheck.note: Minutes 1.5 to 6. Sneak-peek puzzles: two puzzles on the key idea of today, which the children have NOT learnt yet. Say out loud (about 28 words): "Two sneak-peek puzzles on ideas we have not learnt yet. Guessing is welcome, so is I do not know. Nobody is marked. Show your paper to me only." Question 1 is an access question: any child can try it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone has a first win (about 45 seconds). Question 2 is the thinking question (about 90 seconds). Then about 2 minutes for the answers slide and the move on. Answers are PRIVATE: each child holds their own paper to the camera for you only, or writes it on their own paper and shows only you on camera. Do not raise whiteboards together, do not read answers out, do not name children. Q1 answer: 1/2 (one half). Listen for: Equal parts matter. Folding on camera is welcome. This is a first win for everyone. Q2 answer: Ali (1/5). The same prata cut into fewer parts gives bigger parts. Listen for: Many children say 1/8 because 8 is bigger. Draw two strips, one cut in 5 and one cut in 8, and compare. A drawing is a good answer. At the end click to show the answers as "one way to think about it", without saying who had what. Ask only for volunteers: "Would anyone like to tell us how they started?" Invite the WHOLE group at once, never one child: "When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Never announce who is on which page. Pairs are not split unless both children agree. Children can move either way at any time. Everyone joins explore, the mini-lesson, the check-together slides and talk time.

p2l7-warm1.note: Minutes 6 to 8.5. Fair or not fair? Point to one snack at a time: "Ali and Mei share this. Is it fair? Thumbs up or thumbs down." Then click to show the answer (clicks go pizza, prata, cake, pancake: four snacks only; the kaya toast and chocolate bar are spare). Ask every time: "How do you know?" Listen for "the parts are the same size" (fair) and "one part is bigger" (not fair). Answers: pizza fair (cut through the middle: 2 halves); prata not fair (the cut is not through the middle); cake fair (3 equal parts: thirds); pancake not fair (all cuts go through the middle, but 2 pieces are small and 2 are big). The pancake is the tricky one: cutting through the middle is not enough, the pieces must be the same size. Today's big word: EQUAL parts. A game of about 2.5 minutes: stop it on the clock even if the game is not finished.

p2l7-warm2.note: Minutes 8.5 to 10.5. Read each question aloud, give thinking time, take answers on whiteboards, then click to show. Ask "How do you know?" each time. Answers: 1) one quarter, written 1/4 ("1 of 4 equal parts") 2) 3. Spare questions in the guide table: how many halves make 1 whole (2); a cake cut into 5 equal pieces, 1 piece is one fifth, 1/5; 2 of 7 equal parts shaded is 2/7. Show how we write it: the bottom number is how many EQUAL parts the whole has, the top number is how many we take. Watch for children who write shaded over not shaded: ask "How many parts are there altogether?" Ask quick questions 1 and 3 only (about 2 minutes): children answer by thumbs, hands, not by naming a child. The other questions are spare.

p2l7-explore1.note: Minutes 10.5 to 19.5. The strips are cut before the lesson (kit at minute 0). Each child folds three strips (halves, quarters, eighths) and writes the fraction on one part of each, not all 15; pairs compare. Show how to fold in half by matching the ends. Quarters: fold in half, then in half again. Eighths: in half three times. Children line the strips up under each other, left ends together. Folding a strip into 3 equal parts is NOT part of the pair task any more: it is the Go further box at the foot of this slide and a take-home. Thirds are hard on purpose (roll the strip into an S and flatten it, then check the 3 parts are the same length). Say if a child tries: "Thirds are tricky for everybody, grown-ups too. A strip that does not come out equal is a good try, not a mistake." Nothing is marked. Fractions are written as 1/2 on slides and as stacked fractions in the workbook: both mean the same. Go further (a second what-if, so nobody waits) is the box at the foot of this slide; the question is also posted in the chat when the pairs go to their breakout rooms. It is for ANY child who finishes the explore task or wants more: say it to the whole group as a choice, never as a prize, and never name who tries it. Pairs stay together unless both children agree to split. Answer: Thirds: fold and adjust until the 3 parts match, then check one part on top of another. 3 sixths make a half and 2 sixths make a third. Take it at the debrief only if a pair offers it.

p2l7-explore2.note: Minutes 19.5 to 23.5. Let pairs keep working, then gather them. Answers: 1) 1/4 is bigger. The strip is the same length, but cut into 4 parts instead of 8, so each part is longer. Put the strips together to show it. 2) 2 eighths fit on 1 quarter; 4 quarters make 1 whole (and 8 eighths make 1 whole). (The thirds question goes with the Go further box and the take-home.) Ask: "Is 1/8 bigger because 8 is bigger than 4?" No! More parts means each part is smaller. We use this idea all lesson. Keep it moving (about 4 minutes in all): ask "how do you know?" on question 2 only; about 15 seconds of talk on the other questions.

p2l7-teach1.note: Minutes 23.5 to 25.5. Teach. Ask first: "Ali says both bars are cut into thirds. Do you agree?" Take votes. Click 1: count the parts together: 3 and 3. Click 2: "Are they the same size?" Bar A yes, bar B no: one part is much bigger. Click 3: only equal parts get a fraction name. "One third means 1 of 3 EQUAL parts." Click 4: equal parts can look different. Each rectangle is cut into 2 equal parts: down the middle, across the middle, or corner to corner (fold one triangle onto the other: they match). Think-aloud: "Before I name a fraction, I check two things: how many parts, and are they all the same size? If they are not the same size, I cannot use a fraction name."

p2l7-we1.note: Minutes 25.5 to 28.5. Click to reveal each step; ask the group to predict before each click. Think-aloud: "First I check the parts are equal. They are. I count all the parts: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Five equal parts are called fifths, so 5 goes at the bottom. Now I count the shaded parts: 3. That goes on top: three fifths. The parts that are not shaded: 2, so two fifths." Say: "The bottom number tells us how many equal parts make the whole. The top number tells us how many parts we are talking about." The check: 3 fifths and 2 fifths make 5 fifths, the whole bar. Watch for 3/2 (shaded over not shaded).

p2l7-try1.note: Minutes 28.5 to 30. Whiteboards face down until 3, 2, 1 (or show only the tutor; never read a board out), then click. a) 3 equal parts, 2 shaded: 2/3 shaded, 1/3 not shaded. b) 12 equal parts (twelfths); count the shaded ones carefully, they are not next to each other: 5, so 5/12 shaded and 7/12 not shaded (5 + 7 = 12). (The old item c, the unequal parts trap, is dropped: worksheet Q1 B and D are the same idea.)

p2l7-we2.note: Minutes 30 to 33. Click through. Hold up the folded strips from Explore. Think-aloud: "All the bars are the same length, so it is the same whole. One half is 1 of 2 parts. One sixth is 1 of 6 parts. When I cut the same whole into more parts, each part gets smaller. So one sixth is the smallest and one half is the biggest." Story: "One pizza for 2 children, or one pizza for 6 children: when do you get a bigger slice?" Common mistake: "1/6 is bigger because 6 is bigger than 2". Answer with the strips, not just words. Only compare like this when the wholes are the same size. SAME BOTTOM NUMBER (the old we3 slide, merged here): both are sevenths, so every part is the same size; 5 sevenths is more than 2 sevenths, like counting apples. Ask: "Which is bigger, 4/9 or 7/9?" (7/9, more ninths).

p2l7-try2.note: Minutes 33 to 34.5. Whiteboards, then click. a) 1/5: the same whole cut into 5 parts gives bigger parts than cut into 10. b) 8/11: both are elevenths, and 8 elevenths is more than 3 elevenths. Ask a child to explain a without using the words "bigger number". (Item c, smallest first, is dropped: worksheet Q3b.)

p2l7-key.note: Minutes 34.5 to 35.5. Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Naming a fraction when the parts are not equal (Q1 B and D): ask "Are all 4 parts the same size?" (2) Thinking 1/6 is bigger than 1/4 because 6 is bigger than 4 (Q3): fold or draw the strips. (3) Adding the bottom numbers too: 2/5 + 1/5 written as 3/10 (Q4). The parts are still fifths, so only the top numbers are added. (4) Writing shaded over not shaded (3/5 instead of 3/8).

p2l7-break.note: Minutes 35.5 to 38.5. Three minutes: two of movement, one for a drink of water. Face the screen to start. A half turn: you face the back. A quarter turn: you face the side. Three quarter turns: the other side. Try "two quarter turns" (the same as a half turn!). Online: children stay in view of the camera.

p2l7-ws1.note: Minutes 38.5 to 52.5. Pairs work together. Ask "How do you know?" before giving any help. For Q1, give pairs a paper square to fold if they are unsure about E (corner to corner). For Q3c ask "What does the 6 tell us?" The explanation in Q1(a) is marked ★ take-home on the page: children do it at home. Say once, to everyone: "After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." Never say who is on which page. Invite the WHOLE group at once, never one child: "When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Pairs are not split unless both children agree.

p2l7-ws1ans.note: Minutes 52.5 to 55. Click each answer after a pair explains theirs. Q1: F surprises many children: the triangle cut by joining the middles of its sides makes 4 triangles that are all the same size, the middle one is just turned upside down. E: the 4 triangles of a square cut corner to corner are all the same. B: the cuts do not go through the middle. D: the strips are different widths. Q2c: count the shaded squares one by one: 7 of 10. Q3b: more parts means smaller parts, so tenths are smallest. Q1(a) (explain one shape that is not quarters) is a take-home star: the answer is B or D, with the reason above.

p2l7-teachadd.note: Minutes 55 to 57. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4 adds and takes away fractions). Click 1: colour 2 ninths. Click 2: colour 4 more. Click 3: count the coloured parts: 6. Think-aloud: "Two ninths and four ninths. Ninths are the name of the parts, like apples. 2 apples and 4 apples are 6 apples. 2 ninths and 4 ninths are 6 ninths. The parts do not change size, so it stays ninths." Then the side question: 9 ninths make the whole bar, so 3 more ninths are needed. Taking away works the same way: 6/9 − 2/9 = 4/9. Big mistake to stop: 2/9 + 4/9 = 6/18. Show that 6/18 would mean the parts became smaller, which did not happen.

p2l7-teachstory.note: Minutes 57 to 58.5. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q5 is a cake story with different numbers). Click through. Think-aloud: "The cake has 10 equal pieces, so I draw a bar of 10 parts: each part is one tenth. Ben eats 4: I colour 4. Siti eats 3: I colour 3 more in a new colour. Eaten: 4 tenths and 3 tenths make 7 tenths. Left: the white parts: 3 tenths." Ask: "Who ate more? How much more?" (Ben, 1/10 more). Always check that eaten and left make the whole.

p2l7-teachsame.note: Minutes 58.5 to 59.5. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q6 compares a quarter with eighths). Use the folded strips from Explore: lay the halves strip on the eighths strip. Click 1: one half covers 4 eighths. Click 2: Ben ate 3 eighths, Mei ate the same as 4 eighths, so Mei ate more. Think-aloud: "Halves and eighths are different parts, so I cannot just look at the numbers. I draw the same whole twice, the same length, and line the parts up." Ask: "What if Mei's pizza were tiny?" Then we cannot compare like this: the wholes must be the same size. Equivalent fractions are a P3 topic: show that one half covers 4 eighths with the lined-up strips only, and do not write 1/2 = 4/8 as a rule.

p2l7-ws2.note: Minutes 59.5 to 71. Children work alone. Q4(d) and Q4(e) are marked ★ take-home on the page: children do them at home. Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson. For Q6, check children draw both bars the same length. Tutor rule at minute 59.5: if the clock is more than 2 minutes late, drop the last Core question of page 2 to take-home (children draw a star beside it). Never shorten talk time, the exit ticket, looking back or the closing. Questions marked with a star and the words take-home on the page are done at home; their answers are still on the check-together slide.

p2l7-ws2ans.note: Minutes 71 to 73.5. Click each answer after a child explains (answer lines only). Q4(d) and Q4(e) are take-home stars: the answers stay here so children can mark them at home. Q4d: 6 sixths make 1 whole, so 5/6 more. Q4e: 7 tenths take away 3 tenths is 4 tenths. Q5: 2 + 3 = 5 slices eaten (5/8); 8 − 5 = 3 left (3/8); Mei ate 3 slices, Ali 2: Mei ate 1/8 more. Q6: the pizzas are the same size; Ravi's 1 quarter covers 2 eighths, Siti ate 3 eighths.

p2l7-stretch.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time). Open to any child who chooses it (the choice after question 3 on the worksheet). These are the SAME four questions as the printed Think harder page: the slide shows 1 to 3 and question 4 is on the page only. Never announce who is working on which page. Answers: 1) 1/12, 1/5, 1/3, 1/2 2) No. Eighths are smaller than fifths (the more equal parts, the smaller each part). So 3 eighths is less than 3 fifths: 3/5 is bigger than 3/8. 3) No. 3 eighths and 2 eighths make 5 eighths: 5/8. The parts are still eighths, like 3 apples and 2 apples make 5 apples. Adding the bottom numbers would change the size of the parts. 4) (Question: Ali says: “Half of my pizza is bigger than half of your pizza.” Can he be right? Explain.) Yes, if his pizza is bigger. Halves of different-size wholes are different sizes.

p2l7-challenge.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time). Use as a pair go-further or in talk time. Ask for the reason every time. More are in the question bank. Answers: 1) 1/5 and 1/6. 2) Ben gets 3/12 (and Ali 5/12).

p2l7-chdiag.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time). Show after pairs have tried the Go further, or if they are stuck. The diagrams show the problem, not the answer. Ask: What do you notice? What do we know? What do we not know yet? Can you draw it? Answers are in the Go further slide notes.

p2l7-chwalk.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time). Use after pairs have tried. Q1: list the unit fractions in order with bars: 1/4, 1/5, 1/6, 1/7. Only 1/5 and 1/6 are between. Children who say 1/3 or 1/8 have turned the rule round: show the strips. Q2 uses the "take away the extra, share, give it back" idea: 8 pieces, take away 2, share 6 as 3 and 3, give the 2 to Ali. Ben 3/12, Ali 5/12, Mei 4/12.

p2l7-talk.note: Minutes 76.5 to 81.5. Pairs talk for 90 seconds, then two volunteers share. Answer: when the wholes are the same size, yes, 1/2 is bigger. But half of a small cupcake is less than a quarter of a big cake! Fractions only compare like this when the wholes are the same. Praise the reasons, not only the answers. Talk time rules: you choose volunteers first ("Who would like to share?"); never cold-call a child by name; any child may say pass; no public tallies, scores or rankings.

p2l7-exit.note: Minutes 81.5 to 86.5. Answers: 1/7 is bigger (the same whole cut into fewer parts, so each part is bigger). 2/9 + 5/9 = 7/9. Children who write 7/18 added the bottom numbers: ask "What size are the parts?" Extension: How much more than 7/9 makes 1 whole? (2/9). Hold-up: children hold their slips up one at a time (never all together); the answer is on the next click. About 2 minutes of child work.

p2l7-reflect.note: Minutes 86.5 to 88.5. Looking back: about 2 minutes, in the box on the page called "Before you go: Investigation and Looking back" (the page after worksheet page 2; every child reaches it). Children finish one line, two lines or all three, and tick what helped. A pass is always allowed. No marks and no wrong answers. Tutor script: SAY: Looking back takes 2 minutes. Find the box called Looking back on the page “Before you go: Investigation and Looking back”. Finish one line, two lines or all three, and tick what helped you. You may pass on any line. If you tick "I am still stuck", your tutor will check in during the session. DO: Nothing is collected in front of the group and nobody has to read theirs out. The tutor may read a box while stamping journals (never by private message), and checks in on a child who ticked still stuck during the open session, for example by a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal with a parent nearby, for example "I saw you drew it when you got stuck". A child may volunteer one sentence, never by name unless they choose to. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the next open session (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby). Praise the strategy, not the speed. Closing and stamps take the last minute and a half (88.5 to 90).
